what: A global store is one shared place in the browser for client state - things only the app knows, like a theme, a sidebar, a wizard step or a draft - so far-apart components can read and change it without passing props down. Libraries such as Zustand and Redux Toolkit give it a small API, and components subscribe to just the slice they need.
like: Like a classroom notice board everyone can read and pin to, so nobody has to pass notes from desk to desk.
why: Distant components share state without prop drilling
Updates go through named actions, so changes are easy to trace and debug
Selectors keep re-renders small, so the UI stays fast

steps.d: Create the store in one module. In Zustand you call create() with state and actions together; in Redux Toolkit you use configureStore and createSlice.
A component passes a selector, so it re-renders only when the piece it selected changes. This is the main performance lever.
Events call a setter (Zustand) or dispatch a named action (Redux). Redux reducers stay pure and Immer lets you write update code that looks like mutation.
Compute totals and filtered lists from the store in selectors instead of storing them twice, so two copies can never disagree.
Persist middleware saves chosen fields (partialize) to storage and can migrate old versions. DevTools log each action for debugging.

numbers.l: react.dev principles for structuring state: group related, avoid contradictions, avoid redundant, avoid duplicate, avoid deep nesting
context providers needed to use a Zustand store - the hook works in any component
core Redux Toolkit APIs to start: configureStore and createSlice

choices.d: Zustand is a tiny hook-based store with no boilerplate; Redux Toolkit adds strict structure, DevTools and a big ecosystem, which suits large teams. Redux docs say that if you write Redux today you should use Redux Toolkit.
Keep state next to where it is used first. Lift it to a store only when many distant components need it. A global store for everything becomes hidden coupling.

React Context is fine for rarely-changing values such as theme or current user. When a provider value changes, every consumer re-renders, so frequently-changing state belongs in a store with selectors.
Only client state (UI flags, drafts, wizard steps). Server data belongs in a server-state cache, and filters you want shareable belong in the URL.

instead.why: For data that comes from the API - it needs caching, refetching and staleness, which a plain store does not give you
For filters, tabs and pages that should survive refresh and be shareable as a link

breaks.d: Components select the entire state object instead of one slice.
breaks.see: Typing in one input re-renders half the page
breaks.fix: Select the smallest slice; use shallow comparison or split the store

breaks.t: Server data copied into the store
breaks.d: API responses are pushed into the store and kept by hand.
breaks.see: Stale lists, manual loading flags, duplicated entities
breaks.fix: Move fetched data to a server-state cache; keep the store for client-only state

breaks.t: Persisted state from an old version
breaks.d: A new release changes the shape but old localStorage is loaded as-is.
breaks.see: Crashes or blank UI after deploy for returning users
breaks.fix: Use the persist version and migrate options; persist only needed fields

say: I split state by kind: server data in a query cache, shareable view state in the URL, form state in the form library, and only the leftover client state in a small global store.
Components subscribe through selectors so a change re-renders only what read it; I derive values instead of storing them twice.
For persistence I save only the fields that must survive, with a version and a migration so old localStorage cannot crash a new release.

followups.q: Why not just use React Context?
followups.a: Context re-renders every consumer when its value changes. It is great for stable values like theme or user, but fast-changing state is better in a store where components select only their slice.

followups.q: Redux or Zustand for a big team?
followups.a: Both are valid. Redux Toolkit gives enforced structure, DevTools and middleware conventions; Zustand is lighter and quicker to start. I pick by team size and how much structure the team needs, and say so.

today: Redux Toolkit is the official way to write Redux, and the docs treat server data as a job for a separate cache: TanStack Query's own docs note that after moving async data there, the remaining global client state is usually small.

check.q: Which kind of state is a good fit for a global store?
check.a: Client-only UI state such as a sidebar or wizard step
check.why: Server data belongs in a query cache, URL state in the URL; the store holds what only the app knows.

check.q: How do you stop a component re-rendering on unrelated store changes?
check.a: Subscribe with a selector for just the slice it needs
check.why: A component re-renders only when its selected value changes.

check.q: Why derive totals in a selector instead of storing them?
check.a: Two stored copies can drift apart; a derived value cannot
d: Selectors are free to run on a server
check.why: react.dev lists 'avoid redundant state' - anything computable should be computed.
